summaries.example: Imagine a child who has never learned to swim. Diodorus might say that becoming a swimmer is possible only if the child is swimming now or will swim later. If the child never swims, then, in his system, becoming a swimmer was not possible. This can feel surprising because we often call an unused chance a possibility.
summaries.summary: Diodorus Cronus was a philosopher of ancient Greece who became famous for dialectic, the careful testing of arguments. The Stanford Encyclopedia entry focuses especially on his ideas about possibility, time, change, and language. His Master Argument starts with three claims that cannot all stand together: every past truth is necessary, possibility cannot lead to impossibility, and some possible things never happen. Diodorus rejected the third claim. On his view, something is possible exactly when it is true now or will be true later. This makes possibility closely depend on the actual course of time. Diodorus also held that bodies, places, and times have basic units with no parts. Using this idea, he argued against change happening in the present, while still allowing truths about changes that happened in the past. His ideas about words and meanings were meant to help people argue clearly.
key_ideas: Diodorus Cronus was an ancient Greek thinker known for clever arguments and work on logic.
His Master Argument connects possibility with the past and the future.
He said that a possible truth must either be true now or become true later.
His view of possibility led some people to connect his philosophy with fatalism.
He described basic, partless units of bodies, space, and time.
Scholars study how his ideas about time and parts supported his arguments against change.
summaries.why_it_matters: Diodorus shows how one question can affect many areas of philosophy. If possibility depends only on what is or will be true, then ideas about time also affect ideas about freedom and fate. His arguments also show why philosophers care about small details in words such as “possible,” “past,” and “change.” Studying him helps us see that an argument can be clever and important even when people disagree about its conclusion.

important_terms.definition: A way of discussing an idea by asking questions, giving answers, and testing whether an argument works.
A statement about what can happen, must happen, or might happen.
Diodorus's famous argument about the past, possibility, and what will happen.
The view that what happens is fixed in a way that leaves no room for some kinds of alternatives.
The idea that the smallest parts of bodies, places, or times have no smaller parts inside them.

Does knowing what will happen make it impossible for anything else to happen?
Can a thing change if each moment is a separate, indivisible unit?
Should a word always have just one meaning?

summaries.example: Suppose a person is not now in Corinth and never will be there. Under Diodorean possibility, “that person is in Corinth” is not merely false; it is impossible. If the person is there now or will be there later, the statement is possible. This differs from a more familiar view, on which an event might be possible even if it never occurs. The example therefore makes the debate about modality depend on how possibility is related to time.
summaries.summary: Diodorus Cronus was an influential ancient dialectician whose surviving views connect logic, metaphysics, physics, and philosophy of language. The central issue is the Master Argument. Its reported premises are that every past truth is necessary, that the possible cannot entail the impossible, and that some possible truth is neither true nor destined to become true. Diodorus uses the first two to deny the third. His resulting account says that a proposition is possible exactly when it is true now or will be true. This is not the ordinary idea that an unrealized alternative can still be possible. It makes modality depend on the actual timeline and is therefore often linked with fatalism or logical determinism. The entry notes disagreement about whether Diodorean modalities permit limited forms of future contingency and whether those forms are enough for freedom. Diodorus is also associated with atomism: bodies, places, and times have indivisible simples. This helps explain arguments denying present motion and other present changes, although he accepts some past-tense truths about change. His treatment of conditionals is stronger than a simple material conditional and has been interpreted in several ways. Finally, his views about univocal meaning and naming address how dialectical arguments can avoid ambiguity and paradox. The entry also emphasizes that the evidence does not settle every question about his school affiliation or the exact formulation of his arguments.
key_ideas: The Master Argument is presented as an inconsistent triad: past truths are necessary; possibility does not entail impossibility; and some possibilities never become true.
Diodorus rejects the third member and identifies possibility with what is true now or will be true.
His modal system is temporal: knowing the actual truth of a proposition across time determines whether it is possible in the Diodorean sense.
The system is often associated with fatalism, but scholars disagree about whether it permits some future contingencies and what that means for freedom.
Diodorean atomism treats bodies, places, and times as composed of indivisible but extended or durational simples.
His arguments against present change use atomism, while his account of past change distinguishes having changed from presently being in the process of changing.
summaries.why_it_matters: Diodorus matters because his philosophy shows how theories of time, possibility, logic, physical structure, and language can form a connected system. His account challenges the assumption that an unrealized possibility is automatically genuine. His arguments also anticipate enduring questions: whether the past is necessary, whether the future is open, whether freedom requires the ability to do otherwise, and whether language can support reliable reasoning. Because the evidence comes through later reports and interpretations, studying Diodorus also teaches intellectual caution: reconstructing an ancient philosopher requires separating what is directly reported from what scholars infer.

important_terms.definition: A method of reasoning through questions and answers, often by drawing consequences from assumptions accepted by an opponent.
A claim about possibility, necessity, or contingency; in this entry, modal claims are closely connected with temporal claims.
The argument reported as using three apparently incompatible principles to support Diodorus’s account of possibility.
The principle that every past truth is necessary, one of the three claims in the reported Master Argument.
Diodorus’s claim that a proposition is possible if and only if it is true now or will be true.
The view that events are settled in a way that excludes certain alternatives; scholars disagree about how strongly Diodorus’s system is deterministic.
The theory that bodies, space, and time contain basic units that have no parts, including minima of time and space.
A conditional that, according to a common interpretation, remains true at every time rather than merely avoiding a true antecedent followed by a false consequent at one time.

questions_to_think_about: Does a proposition count as possible only when it eventually becomes true?
Is an unchangeable past truth necessarily true, or could it be contingent but beyond our power to alter?
Can a system be deterministic while still allowing some descriptions of future contingency?
What problems arise when a conditional must hold not just now, but across all times?
Can precise speaker intention prevent ambiguity, or can words have meanings beyond what a speaker intends?

summaries.example: Think about a school play. A student is not playing the lead today, and will never play it in any later performance. In everyday speech, you might still say the student could have played the lead. Diodorus’s account is stricter: the student playing the lead is possible only if the student is playing it now or will play it later. If it never happens, it was not possible in his technical sense. This is why his view can seem connected to fate.
summaries.summary: Diodorus Cronus was an ancient Greek philosopher admired for his skill in dialectic and logic. His best-known contribution is the Master Argument, which concerns necessity, possibility, and time. The argument is reported through three claims: every past truth is necessary; a possible claim cannot lead to an impossible result; and at least one possible claim never becomes true. Diodorus keeps the first two and rejects the third. His own position is that a claim is possible if it is true now or will be true later. For example, something that never happens is not possible in his special sense, even if ordinary people might call it an unused opportunity. This view is often called fatalist because it seems to leave little room for alternatives. However, the entry explains that scholars disagree about exactly how deterministic the system is and about whether it permits limited kinds of future contingency. Diodorus also held a form of atomism. Bodies, places, and times are made from simple units that cannot be divided. This supports arguments against present motion and other present changes. He did not simply deny every statement about change: he allowed that something may have moved, while denying that it is ever presently moving. His work also includes ideas about conditionals, ambiguity, naming, and paradoxes. The surviving evidence is incomplete, so some details of his theories remain debated.
key_ideas: Diodorus was known for dialectic and was associated by current scholarship with a Dialectical School rather than simply the Megaric School.
His Master Argument says that three attractive claims conflict, so at least one must be rejected.
He rejects the claim that something can be possible even though it is never true.
His theory links possibility to the present and future, which raises questions about fate and free choice.
His atomism says that bodies, space, and time have smallest units with no parts.
He argued against change occurring in the present but accepted some truths about changes in the past.
summaries.why_it_matters: Diodorus helps us understand why philosophers connect logic with everyday questions about choices and the future. His position makes us ask whether “possible” means “could happen” or only “will happen at some time.” His arguments about indivisible moments show how a theory about the structure of time can affect views about motion and change. His work on language is also useful because clear definitions are essential in any argument. Studying the disagreements about Diodorus reminds us that interpreting an ancient thinker often involves careful reconstruction rather than certainty.

important_terms.definition: Reasoning through questions and answers to test claims and reveal what follows from them.
A philosophical claim about what is possible, necessary, or merely contingent.
Diodorus’s main argument, which compares three claims about past truth, possibility, and events that never occur.
The idea that what has happened is fixed and cannot be undone; Diodorus’s argument treats past truth as necessary in a stronger sense.
The view that something is possible exactly when it is true now or will become true.
The view that events are fixed so that some alternatives are not genuinely possible.
The idea that reality is built from basic units that cannot be divided into smaller parts.
A statement of the form “if p, then q”; Diodorus’s version is discussed as stronger than a conditional that works only at one moment.

questions_to_think_about: Is a chance still a real possibility if it never happens?
Does “the past cannot be changed” mean that every past truth is necessary?
Could someone be responsible for working hard if the final result is already fixed by what will happen?
Why might indivisible moments make continuous motion difficult to explain?
Can a debate fail because two people use the same word with different meanings?
